query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In a single‐phase compositionally complex alloy, brittle behavior can emerge when high strain‐rate or elevated temperature loading induces extreme, dynamic grain refinement leading to a local amorphization of grain boundaries. This process generates nanoporosity and cavitation along high angle grain boundaries that reduces their cohesive strength, triggering intergranular decohesion despite the absence of significant impurity segregation or intermetallic precipitation.
generation.material_initial_state: An initially coarse‐grained, single‐phase high-entropy alloy (e.g., equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi) with a stable solid-solution structure suitable for demanding engineering applications.
generation.intervention: Apply high strain-rate sliding or deformation under controlled conditions (e.g., in ultra-high vacuum) at a moderately elevated temperature to promote dynamic grain refinement while retaining the single-phase state.
generation.conditions: Comparison between samples deformed under low strain-rate (baseline coarse grain, sustained ductility) and those deformed under high strain-rate conditions that promote ultra-nanocrystalline surface layer formation; environmental conditions should minimize oxidation and chemical segregation.
generation.structural_mediator: The high-angle grain boundaries that, under high strain-rate loading, transform via dynamic amorphization and cavitation into ultra-nanocrystalline (or locally amorphous) regions.
generation.mechanism: Under high strain-rate or specific temperature regimes, the conventional dislocation slip mechanism is suppressed in refined grain regions, activating grain boundary sliding and dynamic amorphization. This leads to the formation of nano‐cavities along high angle grain boundaries that reduce interfacial cohesion and facilitate brittle intergranular fracture.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples subjected to high strain-rate deformation will exhibit a significant increase in grain boundary cavitation and a lowered fracture toughness (indicative of brittle behavior) compared to baseline coarse-grained samples, which maintain ductile deformation.
generation.baseline: The alloy in its as-processed coarse-grained, single-phase state exhibits high ductility and work hardening with conventional dislocation slip governing plasticity.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to dominate when strain rates and/or temperatures are sufficient to induce dynamic grain refinement yet remain below levels that would trigger classical intermetallic phase precipitation; it applies primarily under conditions of severe mechanical shear in environments that prevent extrinsic chemical modifications.
generation.uncertainty: The exact strain-rate and temperature thresholds for the onset of dynamic amorphization and nanocavitation, as well as the critical refined grain size necessary for brittle behavior to emerge, are not quantitatively established and require further empirical determination.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical single-phase high-entropy alloy specimens in a controlled ultra-high vacuum environment. Subject one set to low strain-rate deformation (baseline) and another to high strain-rate sliding deformation at moderately elevated temperatures. Use in-situ transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) to monitor the evolution of the grain size and the formation of intergranular nanocavities. Measure macroscopic fracture toughness and perform digital image correlation to capture strain localization.
measurements: Grain size and grain boundary structure (via STEM/TEM)
Presence and distribution of nanoporosity or cavitation features
Stress-strain curves and fracture toughness values
Friction coefficient and surface shear strength measurements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If high strain-rate deformed samples do not exhibit a significant reduction in grain size at grain boundaries, absence of localized nanocavitation/amorphization, and no measurable decrease in fracture toughness compared to the baseline, then the hypothesis that dynamic grain boundary decohesion is responsible for emergent brittle behavior is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The CALPHAD calculations indicate that oxygen can substantially affect the phase stability in Ti-V-Nb-Ta. In the absence of oxygen, equimolar Ti-V-Nb-Ta is predicted to exhibit a single-phase BCC structure, while trace levels of oxygen facilitate the formation of the α-Ti phase at the aging temperature, consistent with oxygen’s role as an α-stabilizer in Ti alloy (). As nitrogen is also an α-stabilizer in Ti alloys, it may play a similar role to oxygen in facilitating the formation of α-Ti phase in the Ti-V-Nb-Ta. Grain boundary α-Ti precipitates are observed to nucleate initially, followed by the formation of intragranular precipitates and the emergence of PFZs adjacent to the grain boundaries. The experimental characterization and equilibrium phase calculations lead to the inference that the formation of PFZ in the Ti-V-Nb-Ta system is the result of diffusion of Ti and major interstitials (O and N) to grain boundaries, with subsequent formation of nitrogen- and oxygen-rich α-Ti precipitates at the aging temperature. cited_evidence.text: Microstructural stability is one of the most important factors for alloys to be used at elevated temperatures. A stable alloy can maintain its properties without substantial changes, even after extended periods of service (). The minor presence of impurity interstitials, e.g., nitrogen and oxygen, in the equimolar Ti-V-Nb-Ta alloy studied was found to introduce uncertainties in its mechanical properties at the aging temperature by facilitating phase segregation at the nanoscale and reducing the solid strengthening effect. Furthermore, the depletion of impurity interstitials in regions adjacent to grain boundaries leads to the formation of PFZs. This spatially confined compositional variation nearby grain boundaries creates very high local electrochemical and mechanical contrast, often affecting the alloy’s corrosion and mechanical properties (). To improve the stability of RHEAs for high-temperature applications, the impurities must be better controlled. AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties

The Hall-Petch equation, σy=σ0+k⋅d−1/2, is fit to the Luo data only, and agrees reasonably well with the nano-grained estimate from Schuh, et al.. Recent work has shown that low friction of bare metals, in the range μ≅0.2−0.5, can be explained as the dynamic softening (i.e. inverse Hall-Petch behavior) of surfaces due to highly surface-localized, shear-induced severe plastic deformation,,. This is well described by a recently proposed predictive model that explains the low shear strength and friction coefficients of bare metals and alloys. This model of grain size-dependent shear strength requires no fitting parameters and is based exclusively on materials properties and physically meaningful input parameters like temperature and shear rate.
